name: Private credit stress
value: BDCs at steep NAV discounts; no forced sales
summary: Listed BDCs trade well below NAV and semi-liquid funds cap redemptions; no forced sales or bank losses found
state: Listed business development companies have traded at wide discounts to reported NAV through 2026, and several large semi-liquid funds have limited quarterly redemptions to 5% of assets (Mercer Capital). A Boston Fed study found payment-in-kind interest in BDC loans rose to about 10% by early 2026, but put bank commitments to BDCs below 2% of large banks' Tier 1 capital. Searches on 14 Nov found no simultaneous wave of gates, forced asset sales or losses spreading to banks or insurers since the 13 Nov reports, so Watch holds.
for_you: Investors in semi-liquid private credit funds and non-traded BDCs are most exposed: withdrawals can be capped at 5% a quarter and listed prices can sit well below reported values. Wider banking and insurance markets show no sign of contagion so far.
rubric_hit: Watch: listed BDCs at wide NAV discounts and funds limiting redemptions; no multi-fund gating, forced sales or bank losses (Alert)

sources.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston — Early warning signals in private credit? What BDC portfolios reveal
Mercer Capital — Public prices, private marks: what BDC discounts are signalling

why: Private credit has grown fast outside bank regulation; its losses surface late and can spill into banks, insurers and pension funds.
drivers: Defaults among leveraged mid-sized borrowers, payment-in-kind interest, fund redemption requests, bank lending to funds.

rubric.alert: Several large funds gate at once, forced asset sales, or losses spreading to banks or insurers.
rubric.watch: A large fund limits redemptions, listed BDCs trade at wide discounts to NAV, or a cluster of borrower defaults with heavy losses.
rubric.normal: No notable fund gates, defaults or markdowns beyond the routine.
